summary: Specifies several basic forward error correction schemes for the Reliable Multicast Transport building block, including the compact no-code, small block, large block, expandable, and small block systematic schemes. This is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3452 and RFC 3695.

eli5.summary: Send extra repair pieces along with the data, so if some pieces get lost the receiver can fill the gaps without asking again. This memo lists simple ways to do that.

questions: forward error correction for reliable multicast
what is forward error correction in rmt

subtitle: Four simple schemes that say how to label and describe repair data for reliable multicast.

tldr.problem: Reliable multicast senders add forward error correction (FEC) so receivers can recover lost packets without asking for resends, but every content delivery protocol needs a precise format for labeling the pieces.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four FEC schemes, each with a fixed FEC Payload ID layout, FEC Object Transmission Information and an FEC Encoding ID (0, 128, 129 and 130). Only the Compact No-Code scheme specifies how data is actually sent; the other three leave the code itself to specific instances.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3695 and takes over the FEC schemes of RFC 3452, which were previously Experimental. It stays backwards compatible, with one new rule that all encoding symbols of an object have the same length.

today: RFC 5445 is a Proposed Standard from March 2009 and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 3695 and takes over the FEC schemes of RFC 3452.

sections.title: Four Schemes for One Building Block
sections.content:
RFC 5445 specifies four FEC Schemes that follow the requirements of the FEC building block in RFC 5052: the Compact No-Code scheme, the Small Block, Large Block, and Expandable scheme, the Small Block Systematic scheme and the Compact scheme. It inherits the context, language and restrictions of that building block and uses the terminology of RFC 3453.

The same schemes first appeared in RFC 3452 and RFC 3695, both in the Experimental category. This Proposed Standard obsoletes RFC 3695. RFC 3452 had already been obsoleted by RFC 5052, so this document takes over the parts of it that RFC 5052 did not include. Integer fields in all the schemes are encoded in network byte order.
sections.eli5: Think of a shipping company with four standard kinds of labeled boxes. This memo describes the labels and the boxes, not the stuff you pack inside.

sections.title: Fully-Specified and Under-Specified Schemes
sections.content:
The RFC sorts its schemes into two kinds. The Compact No-Code scheme is Fully-Specified: everything needed to interoperate is written down. The other three are Under-Specified: this document defines the packet and object formats, but the actual FEC code and the mapping of Encoding Symbol IDs to encoding symbols belong to specific instances, identified by an FEC Instance ID. Their details may even be proprietary.

Each scheme is described the same way: the FEC Payload ID carried in each packet, the FEC Object Transmission Information (OTI) that describes the object, the procedures, and the FEC code specification. The OTI has a mandatory part (the FEC Encoding ID), a common part and a scheme-specific part.
sections.eli5: Some boxes come with full packing instructions. Others only tell you how to label the box, and the packing instructions come from whoever uses it.

sections.title: Compact No-Code and Compact FEC Scheme
sections.content:
The Compact No-Code scheme (FEC Encoding ID 0) needs no FEC coding at all. It exists mainly to allow simple interoperability testing between implementations. Its FEC Payload ID is a 16-bit Source Block Number plus a 16-bit Encoding Symbol ID. Source block numbers can be unique or non-unique within an object; which mode is used is communicated out of band. In unique mode there are at most 2^16 source blocks, and in non-unique mode packets for two different source blocks with the same number SHOULD NOT be sent within a shorter interval than the transport time of a source block.

Each encoding symbol is a run of consecutive bytes of the source block. With source block length X and symbol length L, N is X/L rounded up, and symbol Y holds bytes L*Y through L*(Y+1)-1. The RFC's example: X = 20,400 and L = 1,000, so symbol 20 holds bytes 20,000 to 20,399 and the other 600 bytes are padded with zeroes.

The Compact FEC scheme (ID 130) is similar in spirit but allows a real, Under-Specified FEC code. It reuses the Compact No-Code payload ID format, the common OTI of the Small Block scheme and its scheme-specific OTI.
sections.eli5: The simplest scheme just cuts the data into equal slices and numbers them. The last slice may be short, so it gets blank filler. The Compact scheme works the same way, but the slices may be made with a clever recipe.

sections.title: Small Block, Large Block and Systematic Schemes
sections.content:
The Small Block, Large Block, and Expandable scheme (ID 128) uses a 32-bit Source Block Number and a 32-bit Encoding Symbol ID. The code details are left to specific instances, and the OTI adds a 16-bit FEC Instance ID.

The Small Block Systematic scheme (ID 129) is for codes whose source blocks hold at most 65535 source symbols. Because systematic codes often change the block length, the payload ID carries a 16-bit Source Block Length together with a 32-bit Source Block Number and a 16-bit Encoding Symbol ID. Each encoding symbol is either an original source symbol or a redundant one. Its common OTI also holds a Max-Number-of-Encoding-Symbols value.

For IDs 128, 129 and 130 the scheme-specific OTI starts with a one-octet Length counted in four-octet words, where zero means no instance-specific information (three zero padding bytes then follow). It is optional only if the content delivery protocol signals the total OTI length externally.
sections.eli5: Bigger jobs need bigger label numbers. The systematic scheme also writes the box size on every label, because the boxes change size a lot.

sections.title: Object Transmission Information and Procedures
sections.content:
In the Compact No-Code scheme the Transfer Length is under 2^48 octets, the Encoding Symbol Length under 2^16 octets and the Maximum Source Block Length under 2^32 symbols, packed as 48, 16 and 32 bits. A Reserved field MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt. All encoding symbols of an object MUST have the length given in the OTI, except possibly the last source symbol of the last source block, which MUST be logically padded with zeroes when another symbol is computed from it, although the padding need not be sent.

Schemes 0, 128 and 130 MUST partition the file into source blocks with the algorithm in Section 9.1 of RFC 5052. For scheme 129 that algorithm MAY be used; otherwise the scheme instance MUST specify its own.

For the Compact No-Code scheme a carousel is RECOMMENDED. The sender starts at a random symbol ID Y in [0..N-1], sends symbol Y, and increments Y, wrapping from N-1 back to zero. The receiver keeps a boolean array RECEIVED[0..N-1] and has the whole block once every entry is true.
sections.eli5: The sender walks around and around a circle of numbered pieces, starting at a random spot. The receiver ticks off each piece it catches, and is done when every box is ticked.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says only that this specification does not introduce any further security considerations beyond those described in RFC 5052.
sections.eli5: This memo adds no new safety worries beyond those in the building-block memo it builds on.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC re-assigns the FEC Encoding IDs in the ietf:rmt:fec:encoding name-space: 0 to Compact No-Code and 130 to Compact FEC (both first defined in RFC 3695), and 128 to Small Block, Large Block, and Expandable and 129 to Small Block Systematic FEC Codes (both first defined in RFC 3452). References to the old specifications should be replaced with this document.

Because IDs 128, 129 and 130 are Under-Specified, the document also takes responsibility for the FEC Instance ID registries ietf:rmt:fec:encoding:instance:128, :129 and :130. Values are non-negative numeric indices assigned First Come First Served, subject to the criteria in RFC 5052.
sections.eli5: Each scheme gets a number in an official list, like a locker number, so everyone refers to the same box.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3452 and RFC 3695
sections.content: Section 10 lists three differences. The scheme definitions were updated to meet RFC 5052. Complete OTI encodings are now defined here for each scheme rather than inside content delivery protocol specifications, since the format depends on the scheme. And all encoding symbols of an object must now have the same length, which earlier Compact No-Code and Small Block Systematic specifications did not require. The RFC argues this causes no compatibility problem because no protocols support varying lengths.
sections.eli5: The rules were tidied up, and one new rule was added: all slices must be the same size.
